html:
A 17th century fort at Makassar on the island of Sulawesi, Indonesia, rebuilt by the Dutch after they defeated the sultanate of Gowa. It is one of the best preserved Dutch forts in Asia.

Gowa, ruled from Makassar, was a powerful Muslim trading state that let all comers buy spices and broke the Dutch hold on the trade. Its rulers built a fort on the site around 1634. In 1666 the Dutch East India Company sent Cornelis Speelman, with the Bugis prince Arung Palakka as his ally, against Sultan Hasanuddin. The Treaty of Bongaya of 1667 handed the fort to the Company.

The Dutch rebuilt it between 1673 and 1679 with five bastions and named it after Speelman's home town. It became the centre of Dutch power in eastern Indonesia. The Javanese prince Diponegoro, leader of the Java War, spent his last years imprisoned here and died in 1855. Makassar sailors also kept up the trepang trade to northern Australia.
sum: A 17th century fort at Makassar on the island of Sulawesi, Indonesia, rebuilt by the Dutch after they defeated the sultanate of Gowa. It is one of the best preserved Dutch forts in Asia.
